title: I Saw the TV Glow, Nope, and the "Trap of Elevated Films"

commenti.body: im a little sore bc its pride and im trans and maybe im just triggered... but though i find this argument interesting and worthy of debate, i take particular umbrage at your last statement where you position yourself as some kind of arbiter of how minorities should express their experiences (namely, that their main goal should be capitulating to the least charitable, bigoted reading of their metaphors and more bizarrely, that the "progressive metaphor" is some ploy to attract audiences rather than an attempt at genuine self-expression). beyond that, this analysis assumes absolute knowledge of the intentions of the filmmakers while providing next to no actual discussion of the specific filmmaking techniques that lead to the author's conclusions, preferring instead to broadly reiterate the plot and interject the author's personal interpretation (or fears about potential bigoted interpretations) of the films' deeper meanings.

I think your conclusion on both is deeply flawed. First of all, US is not saying one or the other. It is discussing both. So a huge part of the movie is the question “is there a way to create art that doesn’t exploit someone”, part of a larger conversation happening with Under the Silver Lake, Babylon and the Fablemans as well. 

Secondly, Owen doesn’t seem to miss childhood, in my opinion. His childhood was miserable. He had no friends, a mother that died when he was young, and an abusive father. He goes to eat on the bleachers with an outcast who is several years older than him because there’s nothing else left. So saying that he retreats into this identity as a way to reclaim the feeling of childhood feels completely off base to me. A better question is, why do you think he was so uncomfortable that whole time? Because he was already grappling with his identity.

I think you're trying to simplify both films into allegories, which is not what they are. Just to address one point: I don't think *I Saw the TV Glow* takes place in "reality" at all. The "reality" in which Owen spends most of their time is constructed on a few important levels:

1) It's literally constructed. It's a series of film sets created for the film production *I Saw the TV Glow*. On this level, the world of VHS and Owen working at the arcade is no more or less real than the world of *The Pink Opaque*.

2) The set design persistently and conspicuously mirrors Owen's life and inner world. The walls are scrawled with messages representing and reinforcing Owen's repressions and inner monologue. The world Owen lives in is not an objective space but a subjective one-- the audience only ever sees the world from *Owen's* perspective. And Owen's perspective is characterized by repression and denial.

3) The presentation of the world is mediated, even disrupted, by annotations, such as the superimposed lettering from Owen's tapes. So we are seeing a constructed world, designed to mirror one character's subjectivity, which then has further construction placed on top of it.

Within the context of *I Saw the TV Glow*, reality is mysterious and unknowable. We're not meant to take what we see on screen as 'reality,' and the characters' attempts to escape the world they are in should not be equated with delusion. To go out on a limb, many people take the 'reality' of gender for granted, even though like this film, it's a complex and mediated social-psychological construct. I think you're committing that same error here: you take for granted the reality of the world we're shown, when the whole point of the film is that the reality we're shown is not absolute.

In general, if you're watching a work of art by a minority group you're not in, about said minority group, you should assume that the creator knows more about how to best depict that minority group than you do. Instead of announcing that they regrettably missed the point of their own movie, you should instead question why you react to their art the way you do, and try to consider why they may have done something that you don't yet understand.

I think your take on Nope is pretty flawed and is surprising considering you have that Jordan Peele interview.  You somehow took an interview from him where he says he doesn't want to be pigeon holed as the racism horror director and completely ignored the hilarious point of Keke Palmers opening speech then went on to analyze nope through a racial lens.

Genuine question: are you Black or trans? Not that you have to be to have an opinion on either film, obviously. But there are definitely certain elements in both films that can be difficult to appreciate if you don't relate to them, imo.

"If you were to say the movie is about how people get bored in the suburbs and decide they miss the feeling of being a kid, the attention they got, the tv shows they watched, and just have a breakdown and call that being trans, I'd have a hard time arguing against that."

I wouldn't. But even if someone were to make that argument: so what? Even if these films were perfectly executed in your eyes, without a single loophole for the bigoted audience member to go, "Ah, yes, all my notions about race and gender have been confirmed," it's hard to believe those folks wouldn't find a way to get there anyway. 

That type of thought is irrelevant to the success or failure of the film; it's the whole nature of that kind of thinking. A bigoted person will go into something -- art, film, whatever -- with a preconceived notion, and then they'll search for a way to confirm it with what's there. That's a very different experience than coming into something with a healthy curiosity and openness to different perspectives. A bigoted person isn't coming into I Saw the TV Glow with the mindset of, "I'm curious how this film will convey identity," watch the film, and then (mistakenly) go, "Wow, y'know what? That movie really shined a light on how being trans really is just a mental illness. I feel like I've gained a fresh insight into that experience." If we're being honest, I don't think they're leaving the theater with anything but confusion and frustration, but regardless, they're not looking at these works through an unfiltered, purely analytic thought process. If they were, they'd be able to listen to any of the millions of trans people in the world and ascertain the truth about what it means in a literal instant. But they're not looking for that, and you can't cater a group to a film who aren't watching in good faith to begin with.

Also, how is "I really like this character on a TV show, I really identify with them" shallow if that's a truthful depiction of trans experience? It's just a piece of the pie, not the whole thing, and it's wrong to imply the movie was attempting to simplify EVERYTHING about being trans into that one idea.

Just gonna add my two cents that Nope isn't about Race, it's about how the movie industry assumes it has control over everything - particularly animals - without understanding the danger that involves. 

I think the movie is very explicit about it, and the Peele interview you mentioned is precisely about how he doesn't want to be beholden to his race all the time.

OOP, if you want to actually learn more about this issue of criticizing minorities for falling into bigot stereotypes and are feeling open to a deep dive, I can't recommend Contrapoints' Video Essay "Cringe" enough. She specifically addresses this and some of the finer nuances of why it's so dangerous.

I'm gonna be upfront and say I'm not good at putting my feels into words.

To piggyback off you. My take on nope had nothing to do with racism but rather how far people will go to secure fame (to put it as short as possible.)

Looking up posts about the movie becaue I just watched 'TV Glow' in the theaters a few hours ago and am buzzing about it...

I am very glad I went into the movie blind. It looked interesting and so I avoided ALL media and trailer about it and experienced it blind.

Coincidentally I'm a straight white cis guy, and, I did not put together the trans/LGBTQ messaging until about an hour after the film was over talking with my wife about it.

I was absolutely emotionally hammered about this movie, and my experience of being emotionally hammered had nothing consciously to do with the trans experience. I absolutely adore this movie even more now. The tools that the movie puts to use to pry apart people's feelings works on more levels than just a straight allegory to the trans experience. Although that allegory is, in hindsight, definitely there, and definitely informing the construction of the movie. The writer/director was able to fashion an experience that reached beyond that, into the outsider, into the kids questioning their reality and then becoming adults stuck in that reality, into being human.

Just fucking incredible. I'm glad I didn't know going in.
